source.title: Capturing the learning curves of generic features maps for realistic data sets with a teacher-student model
source.authors: Bruno Loureiro; Cédric Gerbelot; Hugo Cui; Sebastian Goldt; Florent Krzakala; M. M'ezard; Lenka Zdeborov'a

page_placements.theme: Loss, targets and effective rank determine interpolation thresholds

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error as training-sample count changes, including curves it describes as characteristic double descent and a peak near the interpolation point. It uses ridge or logistic regression on feature representations rather than the original deep-network size sweep.
record.gate_note: The study also discusses double-descent results cited from other work; those are not recorded as rows. The epochs in the GAN and Fashion-MNIST experiments identify snapshots of feature maps, not test error measured over training epochs.
record.test_reason: The paper mainly validates a Gaussian covariate theory of learning curves, but its own real-data ridge-regression simulations show test MSE peaking and then falling as sample count n grows. That is a sample-wise non-monotonicity near interpolation, in a new setting: fixed feature maps on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. T3 rather than T2, because it is not a different method aimed at the original deep-network question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but double descent is incidental. The main conclusion is that a Gaussian covariate teacher-student model, solved rigorously, reproduces real-data learning curves for ridge regression with generic feature maps. Universality rests on second-order statistics. The model fails for classification error and logistic regression on real data, and deviates as n approaches the full dataset size.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and applies a Gaussian covariate teacher-student model, with ridge or logistic regression over fixed feature maps; it does not reproduce a deep-network model-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-map choice and training stage of the feature map change the learning curves. The authors also report that agreement can degrade as the sample count approaches the size of the available real-data set, and that classification results can mismatch the theory.

fits_no_version.finding: For small λ the sample-wise test-error peak sits where the linear system becomes invertible. With learned features, Ω's rank drops from full to 380 over 200 training epochs, so the peak location follows feature-covariance rank rather than nominal width d=2352.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the sample-wise double-descent peak is set by the rank (effective dimension) of the feature covariance, not the nominal number of features.

record.problems: Several plotted curve values are not stated in text. The real-data covariance estimates use the finite available dataset, and the authors report deviations when training-sample counts approach that dataset's total size. They also report a mismatch for classification settings where second-order statistics do not determine the error.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 sample-count curves for logistic regression on GAN-generated and real CIFAR10-like data were not extracted because the text does not state a double-descent or peak result for those curves. Figure 6 sample-count plots were also left out: the stated result concerns agreement with theory near the available-data limit, not a reported increase in test error near interpolation.

untested.parts: No sweep of deep-network model size against test error.
Epochs index feature-map snapshots; test error over training time is not measured.
Deep networks trained end-to-end; classification-error measures; dependence on regularization strength.
No capacity sweep. Fig. 5 varies random-feature dimension across curves, but no model-wise result is stated.
No single complexity measure is tested across size, epoch and sample axes.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks, no optimally tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: V3 was originally stated for deep networks; here the evidence is sample-wise peaks for linear or ridge readouts on fixed features, with non-zero ridge λ. All curve values are figure-only. The Fig. 1 double-descent remark is made collectively, so per-curve states rest on where n≈d falls in the plotted range.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of deep-network model size with test error measured against size.
Feature maps taken from different training epochs are compared, but test error over training time for a fixed network is not measured.
The results concern particular ridge- and logistic-regression tasks and feature representations, not all settings near interpolation.
No capacity sweep across model classes is reported; the relevant sweeps vary sample count.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
The study does not test label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number is tested.

relationships.condition: Ridge regression (λ=10^-2) on MNIST odd/even with raw pixels, erf random features (d=1953) or scattering features (d=1953); ridge (λ=10^-5) on Fashion-MNIST with epoch-200 learned features
relationships.reason: The authors report a characteristic double-descent peak at the interpolation transition for Fig. 1, which in these finite-d curves is a sample-wise peak (R1–R3). For Fig. 4 they place the worst-performance peak at the invertibility point, inferred near n≈380 for epoch 200 (R8).
relationships.display_finding: MNIST learning curves peaked at interpolation, while the Fashion-MNIST peak occurred at invertibility, inferred near n ≈ 380 for epoch-200 features.

relation.reason: Its own ridge-regression sample sweeps and discussion of interpolation peaks bear directly on V3.

tranche.reason: The paper validates Gaussian-covariate learning-curve predictions in real-data fixed-feature settings and reports sample-wise interpolation peaks. Double descent is an incidental result in this new setting.

source_check.notes: The epoch-200 peak near n≈380 is inferred from rank and the stated invertibility criterion; no numerical peak MSE is supplied. Appendix D.1 evaluates test error on the whole dataset universe, including the training subsample, and averages over 10 independent subsamples.
